entry.title: The brain behind the recommendation — a guarded LLM on SAP BTP + SAP AI Core
entry.content:
A custom SAP S/4HANA AI use case, built responsibly on SAP BTP + SAP AI Core.

Part 2 of 3 — "AI‑Guided Supplier Selection in SAP S/4HANA". Part 1: the in‑transaction assistant (ME51N). This part: the SAP BTP + AI Core service that decides. Part 3: the standalone RAP + Fiori app. (Prototype / proof‑of‑concept — a custom extension, not standard/embedded functionality. System IDs, hostnames and deployment IDs are masked.)

TL;DR

In Part 1 we dropped an explainable supplier recommendation straight into ME51N's Desired Vendor field. This part answers the obvious question: how does it decide — and how do we stop an LLM from inventing a supplier or leaking data? The short answer: keep the facts in ABAP, keep the AI on a short leash. S/4 computes the KPIs and sends only a shortlist of eligible candidates; a small FastAPI service on SAP BTP builds the prompt, calls SAP AI Core, and — crucially — validates every answer server‑side so a recommended supplier that isn't one of our candidates is rejected outright. No fabricated vendors, no raw history leaving S/4.

Landscape diagram of S4, BTP and AI Core

Why not just call an LLM from ABAP?

You could POST a prompt to a model and parse whatever comes back. In procurement, that's a bad idea for three reasons:

  • Hallucination — a model might confidently name a supplier you never sourced from, or make up a KPI. In a purchase requisition, that's not a quirky demo — it's a wrong PO.
  • Data residency & trust — you don't want raw purchase‑order and goods‑receipt history flowing to an external endpoint.
  • Explainability — a bare "use vendor X" with no reason is one a buyer will (rightly) ignore.

So the design draws a hard line between what must be deterministic (the numbers) and what the AI is actually good at (ranking and explaining in natural language) — and it puts a validation gate between the model and the business.

The split: ABAP computes, the service reasons

On the S/4 side, ZCL_VENDORREC_SERVICE reads the procurement facts for a material and computes, per supplier, the KPIs that matter — on‑time rate, fill rate, average delay — plus a weighted baseline score and rank. Only that shortlist of eligible candidates (a supplier is eligible if it has real history for the material) is sent onward. The raw history never leaves the system.

The BTP service receives those candidates and does the AI‑specific work: prompt → call → validate → derive sourcing. If anything goes wrong, it returns a status, never a guess.

Responsible AI in one line: the model may only rank and explain the candidates we send it — it cannot add, invent, or alter a supplier. Everything else is deterministic ABAP or server‑side checks.

How it works (technical deep‑dive)

From here on it's for the developers. If you're here for the concept, skip to “What's next”.

The contract

S/4 calls one endpoint — POST /recommend — with the candidates; the service returns per‑material recommendations plus a sourcing scenario:

Request : { consolidation_preference, price_intelligence_available, materials:[ { material,
             suppliers:[ { supplier, is_eligible, baseline_score,
                           on_time_rate, fill_rate, avg_delay_days, …, data_warning } ] } ] }
Response: { ai_status, materials:[ { recommended_supplier, recommendation_reason,
             alternative_suppliers[], recommendation_confidence, … } ],
             sourcing_scenario: { type: COMMON|SPLIT, supplier_count, coverage_pct, assignments[] } }

Note what the request is not: no PO numbers, no receipts, no prices — just aggregated metrics per supplier. (price_intelligence_available is false in V1 — price KPIs are deliberately out of scope, so the model reasons on delivery performance only.)

The prompt keeps the model on a leash

The system prompt is explicit about the rules: recommend only from the supplied eligible candidates for each material, don't invent suppliers or KPIs, justify every pick, and respect the buyer's consolidation preference. It asks for strict JSON only:

You are a procurement sourcing advisor. For EACH material recommend the best supplier ONLY from
that material's supplied eligible candidates. Do not invent suppliers, KPI values, or facts…
Return the top alternative suppliers (up to 4), each with a specific 1–2 sentence reason…
Respond with VALID JSON ONLY: { "materials":[ { "recommended_supplier":"", "recommendation_reason":"",
"alternative_suppliers":[…], "recommendation_confidence":"HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW" } ] }

But a prompt is a request, not a guarantee. The guarantee comes next.

The guarantee: server‑side validation

Every response is validated before it's trusted. If the model names a supplier that isn't in the candidate set for that material — or repeats one, or returns an unknown confidence value — the entire response is rejected and the service returns AI_RESPONSE_INVALID. This is the single most important piece of the whole design:

def _validate(parsed: dict, req: RecommendRequest) -> bool:
    # supplier ids we actually sent, per material
    elig = {m.material: {s.supplier for s in m.suppliers if s.is_eligible} for m in req.materials}
    for r in parsed.get("materials", []):
        mat = r.get("material")
        if mat not in elig:
            return False
        rec = r.get("recommended_supplier")
        if not rec or rec not in elig[mat]:          # <- the anti-hallucination gate
            return False
        if r.get("recommendation_confidence") not in ("HIGH", "MEDIUM", "LOW"):
            return False
        seen = {rec}
        for a in r.get("alternative_suppliers", []) or []:
            sid = a.get("supplier")
            if not sid or sid not in elig[mat] or sid in seen:
                return False
            seen.add(sid)
    return True

Because of this gate, the ABAP side can trust that whatever it defaults into the Desired Vendor is a real, eligible supplier — the model gets to be persuasive, never creative with facts.

Single vs. multi‑material: COMMON or SPLIT

For a single PR line the service just returns the per‑material pick (this is the path Part 1 uses). When several materials are requested together, it derives a sourcing scenario deterministically from the validated picks — never left to the LLM:

  • COMMON — one supplier can cover all materials → a single purchase order.
  • SPLIT — no common supplier (or the preference favors best‑fit) → one PO per supplier group.

The consolidation preference is the buyer's lever: CONSOLIDATE (favor one supplier), BEST_FIT (best per material), or BALANCED (consolidate only when the shared supplier stays within ~80% of the best‑per‑material score). supplier_count in the result is literally the number of POs.

Flowchart of the recommend service decision path

When the AI is unavailable or wrong

There is no silent fabrication. Transport/timeout errors → AI_UNAVAILABLE; malformed or invalid JSON → AI_RESPONSE_INVALID. ABAP treats both as "no AI answer" and falls back to the best supplier by history (flagged BASELINE in Part 1). A truncated model response (hit the token limit) is also treated as invalid rather than half‑trusted.

Secure by construction: S/4 → BTP → AI Core

The call chain is authenticated end‑to‑end:

  1. S/4 gets an OAuth2 token from XSUAA (via the SM59 destination — client credentials).
  2. It calls the service over HTTPS with the Bearer token (TLS trust via STRUST).
  3. The BTP app validates the JWT against XSUAA before doing any work.
  4. The app reads its AI Core credentials from a bound service (never in code) and calls the model.

Sequence diagram of the secured call chain

Secrets live only where they belong — the AI Core key in the BTP service binding, the OAuth client secret in the SM59 destination — and only aggregated KPIs ever cross the boundary.

Setting this up yourself? The click‑by‑click for the OAuth 2.0 client‑credentials profile, the STRUST certificate import, and the SM59 destination is standard connectivity, not specific to this use case — so I won't repeat it here. On help.sap.com search "Maintaining OAuth 2.0 Client Profiles" and "Trust Manager (STRUST)"; on SAP Community search "consume BTP API from ABAP OAuth 2.0 client credentials SM59" for step‑by‑step walkthroughs.

A deployment note

This prototype runs gpt‑4o‑mini via SAP AI Core orchestration — swap in whatever model your AI Core hub serves. Richer per‑supplier reasons mean more output tokens, so watch the model's max‑tokens setting: too low and long multi‑material responses get truncated (→ AI_RESPONSE_INVALID). It's an env‑var, not a code change. A mock mode (deterministic top‑baseline, no model call) is handy for local dev and demos without credentials.

What's next

We've now covered the buyer's experience (Part 1) and the brain that powers it (this part). In Part 3 we look at the standalone RAP + Fiori Elements app — the "explore" surface where a buyer can run recommendations across a whole basket of materials, see the COMMON/SPLIT sourcing, and tune the consolidation preference — all on the same engine.

How are you keeping LLMs honest in your SAP scenarios — prompt discipline, server‑side validation, something else? We'd love to compare notes in the comments.

entry.title: The standalone app — exploring supplier recommendations with RAP + Fiori Elements
entry.content:
A custom SAP S/4HANA AI use case, built responsibly on SAP BTP + SAP AI Core.

Part 3 of 3 — "AI‑Guided Supplier Selection in SAP S/4HANA". Part 1: the in‑transaction assistant (ME51N). Part 2: the SAP BTP + AI Core "brain". This part: the standalone RAP + Fiori Elements app. (Prototype / proof‑of‑concept — a custom extension, not standard/embedded functionality. System IDs, hostnames and deployment IDs are masked.)

TL;DR

Same AI, different doorway. In Part 1 the SAP AI Core recommendation lived inside ME51N — the buyer's in‑flow surface. But sometimes you want to step back and explore with the AI: compare suppliers across a whole basket of materials, let the model reason about whether one vendor can cover everything (one PO) or not (several), and tune the sourcing strategy. That's what this standalone RAP + Fiori Elements app does — the same guarded‑LLM engine as Part 1 and Part 2, wrapped in an interactive UI. It's a managed, draft‑enabled business object exposed as an OData V4 UI service, with one action, RankSuppliers, that orchestrates the AI recommendation end to end.

ranked suppliers and the sourcing scenario for a basket of materials

Two surfaces, one engine

Part 1's ME51N assistant is about flow — you're creating a requisition and the best vendor should just be there. This app is about exploration — a buyer or category manager asks, "for these five materials, what's the smartest way to source them?" Same KPIs, same guarded LLM, same validation — but here the answer includes a sourcing scenario across materials, not just a per‑line default.

  ME51N assistant (Part 1) Standalone app (this part)

Mindsetin‑flow, one line at a timeexplore a whole basket
Triggertyping a material in the PRcreate a Run, add materials, press Rank Suppliers
OutputDesired Vendor default + top‑5 popupranked suppliers + COMMON/SPLIT sourcing
Built withclassic BAdIRAP (managed BO) + Fiori Elements

The run header shows the sourcing scenario; items show the ranked suppliers

Annotated object page of a recommendation run

How it works (technical deep‑dive)

From here on it's for the developers. If you're here for the concept, skip to “Wrapping up the series”.

The business object

It's a two‑level managed, draft‑enabled RAP BO:

  • Run (root) — one recommendation run: the consolidation preference, and after ranking, the scenario type, supplier count (= number of POs), coverage %, and AI status.
  • Item (child) — the materials in the run and, after ranking, each material's recommended supplier, reason, and confidence.

Interface CDS (ZI_VENDORREC_RUN / ZI_VENDORREC_ITEM) model the composition; projection CDS (ZC_VENDORREC_RUN / ZC_VENDORREC_ITEM) add the Fiori UI annotations; a service definition + OData V4 UI binding expose it to Fiori Elements. A material value help (ZI_VENDORREC_MAT_VH) gives an F4 that auto‑fills description/plant/group.

Managed draft BO exposed as an OData V4 UI service

One action does the orchestration

The whole recommendation is a single RAP action on the Run — RankSuppliers. Its handler reads the run's items, builds one candidate request per material (via the deterministic engine from Part 2), calls the service once for the whole run (so it can reason about consolidation), then writes the picks back onto the items and the scenario onto the header (handler trimmed for brevity):

METHOD rank_suppliers.
  " Deterministic engine (candidates/KPIs) + thin AI client (calls the BTP service)
  DATA(svc) = NEW zcl_vendorrec_service( ).
  DATA(ai)  = NEW zcl_vendorrec_ai_core( iv_destination = 'Z_VENDORREC_API' ).

  READ ENTITIES OF zi_vendorrec_run IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY Run FIELDS ( ConsolidationPref ) WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys ) RESULT DATA(lt_runs).

  LOOP AT lt_runs INTO DATA(ls_run).
    " read this run's materials
    READ ENTITIES OF zi_vendorrec_run IN LOCAL MODE
      ENTITY Run BY \_Item FIELDS ( Material ) WITH VALUE #( ( %tky = ls_run-%tky ) ) RESULT DATA(lt_items).

    " one candidate request per material (KPIs computed deterministically in ABAP)
    DATA lt_req TYPE zcl_vendorrec_ai_core=>tt_llm_request.
    CLEAR lt_req.
    LOOP AT lt_items INTO DATA(ls_item).
      APPEND svc->build_llm_request( iv_material = ls_item-Material ) TO lt_req.
    ENDLOOP.

    " one call for the whole run -> honors the consolidation preference (COMMON/SPLIT)
    DATA(res) = ai->get_recommendation( it_requests = lt_req
                                        iv_consolidation_preference = ls_run-ConsolidationPref ).

    " write the recommendation back onto each item …
    " … and the scenario summary (type, #POs, coverage, AI status) onto the run header
  ENDLOOP.
ENDMETHOD.

Two things to note: the deterministic KPIs are computed in ABAP (nothing sensitive leaves S/4), and the sourcing scenario is derived server‑side, not by the LLM — exactly the guardrails from Part 2, reused unchanged.

Why RAP here, but a BAdI in ME51N?

Different jobs, different tools. ME51N already exists and the buyer is in it — enhancing it with a BAdI is the least‑intrusive way to add a default. This app is a new object with its own persistence, draft handling, and UI — which is exactly what RAP + Fiori Elements gives you almost for free (draft, locking, OData, List Report/Object Page). Same engine underneath; the right delivery vehicle for each context.

Consolidation preference: the buyer's strategy lever

The Run header carries a consolidation preference dropdown — CONSOLIDATE, BALANCED, BEST_FIT — which flows into the service call and steers the COMMON‑vs‑SPLIT decision (see Part 2). It's the one knob that lets a human set sourcing strategy while the AI does the reasoning: e.g. "prefer one supplier for the whole basket even at a small KPI cost," vs "give me the strongest supplier per material regardless."



Consolidation preference dropdown and the resulting sourcing scenario

Wrapping up the series

Across three parts we built one idea two ways, on one trustworthy engine:

  • Part 1 — ME51N: the recommendation in flow, defaulted into Desired Vendor with an explainable popup, via a supported BAdI.
  • Part 2 — BTP + AI Core: the guarded brain — deterministic KPIs in ABAP, an LLM kept honest by server‑side validation, secure S/4→BTP→AI Core connectivity, and no data leaving S/4 beyond KPIs.
  • Part 3 — RAP + Fiori: the explore surface — a managed draft BO that ranks suppliers across a basket and proposes the sourcing scenario.

The throughline is responsible, custom S/4HANA AI: deterministic where it must be, AI where it adds value, explainable and human‑in‑the‑loop throughout — built on SAP's own AI platform.

Where next? Extending the same pattern to purchase orders (ME21N), adding a price dimension, and turning the decision log into an adoption dashboard are the obvious next steps.

Thanks for reading the series. If you build something with this pattern — or take it somewhere we didn't — we'd genuinely like to hear about it in the comments.

entry.title: Teaching an LLM to Speak ABAP: Lessons from an MCP Server
entry.content:
Note: This is a personal blog about two personal projects: the MCP server and the local Qwen model. The projects, the measurements, and the opinions in this blog are personal. They do not show the position of SAP SE.

Introduction

AI agents can now read, change, check, and activate ABAP code. They do this through MCP servers. An MCP server gives the agent a set of tools. Each tool sends requests to the ABAP system through the ADT REST interface.

The server in this blog is the EPOD ABAP MCP Server. It runs inside Eclipse ADT, or as a standalone server next to ADT for VS Code.

This blog shows the results of measurements: how agents use the tools, and what makes them use the tools well. The last section asks for your ideas.

A local ABAP model

A local ABAP model is also in progress: an open-weight Qwen model with 27B parameters, fine-tuned (supervised fine-tuning) for agent work with these tools. The model runs without a cloud service.

The training data comes from runs of large models on the same tools (teacher runs). Four rules for this data:

  • Do not remove calls from a teacher run. Later steps depend on them.
  • For each task, use the shortest successful run.
  • Remove repeats: the same tool with the same arguments, and calls with no use, for example an ATC run after a check that already said "ok".
  • After a change in the tool results, make the teacher runs again. The training data must show the same result shapes as the server.

The local model is also a good test for the tools. It shows problems that large models hide (Lesson 3).

Lesson 1: Measure where the tokens go

The basis is one ABAP read task with Claude Opus, with the cost read from the proxy dashboard. This is the distribution:

Item Share of cost

What a tool returns (written into the context cache)63%
The context, read again on each call29%
Output of the model4%
Input: prompt, instruction files, tool descriptions3%

Two rules come from this table:

  1. The size of a tool result is the largest cost. Return only the part that the agent needs.
  2. The number of calls is the second cost. Each extra call reads the full context again. One avoided call saves approximately 22 000 tokens in a typical session.

Examples from the measurements:

  • One method: approximately 500 tokens. The full class: approximately 25 000 tokens.
  • Three messages of a message class: 212 bytes. The full message class: 611 KB.
  • One edit cycle went from five calls to one call.

Lesson 2: The unit of change in ABAP is the method, not the line

Many coding agents edit files with an exact text replacement: "find this text, put that text". This works well for files. For ABAP, it causes problems.

A typical change: a call to a new method. In real code, this change also needs:

  • A variable for the result. In classic style, the DATA statement is at the start of the method, far from the call.
  • Error handling: TRY ... CATCH around the call, or RAISING in the method definition.
  • Changes in the lines that use the result.
  • The new method itself: its definition and its implementation.

The change is in several places. With text replacement, the agent must find a unique text for each place. ABAP repeats many lines (ENDIF., ENDMETHOD., CLEAR lv_x.), so the unique text gets longer. At the end, the agent sends almost the full method, with more risk and more calls.

ABAP developers think in objects, methods, and sections. The tools in this blog do the same. The agent asks for "method CALCULATE of class ZCL_X". The tool returns only this method. The agent writes the full method back in one call. The same call activates the object and reads the result again to confirm it.

Lesson 3: The shape of a tool result can make a model loop

After one release of the server, the local model started to loop. It sent the same two calls 9 to 26 times, in 4 of 11 tasks.

The result format caused the loops. For small classes, the method read returned JSON with the full class as one escaped string (\r\n in the text). Large models ignored this. The local model did not know this shape from its training.

The fix had two parts:

  • A tool result that contains ABAP source is plain text.
  • The shape of the result does not change with the size of the object. The model decides what it reads.

The loops stopped. The cost of the test scenarios went down by 3.4%. Unit tests now lock the result format, so a release cannot change it without notice.

Large models can hide such problems. A test with a small model shows them.

Lesson 4: Write tool descriptions like code, and test them

A tool description is the only manual that the model reads. Each description gets a test in a new session, without instruction files, with at least two clients (Claude Code and Codex CLI).

Three rules came from these tests:

  1. A description must work alone. Do not expect an AGENTS.md file to explain the tool.
  2. A description states facts. A sentence like "call tool X after this tool" made models call tool X when it had no use. Now the result says what the state is, and names the tool.
  3. A parameter text states the form and the effect. An error message is only the safety net.

In one test with 10 scenarios, better descriptions changed the result from 8 to 10 passed scenarios. The number of calls went from 18 to 15. For the dictionary objects (data elements, domains, table types), the pass rate went from 2 of 16 to 12 of 12.

Lesson 5: Eclipse ADT is the specification

The first tests ran on a new system. Then the tools ran on older releases. Some object creations and some activations failed.

For the fix, each request was compared with the request that Eclipse ADT sends for the same action: URI, parameters, media types, headers, body, and the next step after the response. Where Eclipse first reads system information (for example the discovery document), the server now reads the same information.

After this change, the defects stopped. Eclipse ADT works with all these releases, so the same requests work too.

Lesson 6: A green build proves nothing about an ADT contract

Live tests on a real system found all contract defects. Unit tests found none of them. For this reason, the gate for each change is a live test.

Two more rules came from real defects:

  • Report success only when the system confirms it. After a write, the tool reads the object again and compares the values.
  • HTTP 404 means that the object is missing. All other errors name the system and the status.

Other features of the server

The server works together with the tools that SAP ships. Its focus is on work that goes beyond one object in one system:

  • Version history and the difference between versions.
  • Compare an object across systems.
  • Transport requests: list, release, and find the request of an object.
  • Where-used lists.
  • Short dumps: list, group, and analyze the cause.
  • Full support for dictionary objects.
  • A read-only mode for each system.

Get the server

  • Project page with installation steps: EPOD ABAP MCP Server update site
  • Eclipse update site URL (Help > Install New Software): https://git.epod.dev/erhan/epod-adt-mcp-updatesite/raw/branch/main/

Your ideas

The aim of this blog is to collect ideas from the community:

  • Which ABAP tasks do you give to an agent today?
  • Where does your agent waste calls or tokens with ABAP?
  • Which result format works best for your model?
  • Do you test your tools with small models? What did you find?

Write your ideas in the comments.

entry.title: ABAP to Full Stack: Making Sense of What’s Behind a Fiori App (OData, Class, Virtual Element)
entry.content:
Hello! I’m Andréa Molina. After more than 20 years in SAP, the new SAP world left me completely lost, so I decided to share my experience and learn together. I’m moving from classic ABAP to the SAP full stack, one real project at a time, drama included.

From overwhelmed to curious, my journey had (and still has) a lot of bumps. You can check my other posts here. I hope you find understanding and empathy here, and maybe a few laughs.

If you’re in the same boat, this series is for you. In this post: I will share my experience creating a List Report (a Fiori floorplan) built on a CDS view exposed as OData V4, with a virtual element calculated by an ABAP class. Plus a plot twist in Step 5.

A bit of background

On my journey I always try to use case studies that are real and will add value to the business. The library and ice cream examples just give me more anxiety and make no sense to me. So this time I’m turning an existing query/infoset (SQ01/SQ02) into a Fiori app, to understand how much effort and time it would take.

So far I have worked with the Basic template and one CDS KPI app, and I knew there were more template options to explore. This time I thought the List Report Page would work best (well, not really, but let’s move forward for now... surprise at Step 5 of this blog).

Before we move on, read this if you are asking "What on earth is List Report Page and Basic Template?"
When you create a new app from a template, you can choose among a lot of frameworks. Each framework provides a set of prebuilt files, structure and more.

You can read more about FloorPlans here: https://www.sap.com/design-system/fiori-design-web/v1-136/page-types/floorplans/when-to-use-which-floorplan

The project

Transform an existing Query/InfoSet (SQ01/SQ02) into a Fiori application. 

Does SAP Make This Easy?

In my research and studying I couldn't find a tool that automatically converts queries into Fiori applications. If you know of a better approach, please share it in the comments. I'd genuinely love to learn. 

The Challenge

… because I have never done before this project

  • Create a CDS view that delivers the data exactly the way I want it to be displayed, with logic and not just selection from the database
  • Create an ABAP class that is called by the CDS
  • Understand how the ABAP class and the CDS work together
  • Create a KPI on top of the report list

The best way to learn: get your hands dirty! A simple learning exercise 

I am suggesting here a very simple example of CDS, class and app: create a List Report Page based on a CDS.

The result should show all the Sales Orders created in the last 30 days and flag the ones created today.

Step 0: Eclipse

The way to create backend objects for apps is using the ABAP Development Tools (ADT) in Eclipse. If you are new here, check this tutorial to set up your Eclipse ADT: https://developers.sap.com/tutorials/abap-install-adt/ 

Step 1: The CDS Views

To get familiar with frontend and backend (together, they make the full stack), here is what is what.

  • Backend: where the data comes from.
  • Frontend: the screen the user interacts with. This part of the development is the backend.

What is backend: Where the data comes from. Put in very simple words.  it's the data that will populate the frontend. 

The CDS will select from I_SalesOrder, and we will use a virtual element (calculated by an ABAP class) to flag the orders created today. It will only return the last 30 days, so we don't select hundreds of records. 🥴 

Why I_SalesOrder and not VBAK?

If you grew up in ECC like I did, you might be asking: why not use VBAK?

  • Tables move, CDS adapts. Moving from ECC to S/4HANA changed a lot of tables. Take VBUK, where we used to read the order status. Its fields now live in VBAK, so every program that selected from VBUK needs to change. But a program reading the status through I_SalesOrder will keep working, because SAP updated the view and left the interface alone. That's the idea behind released CDS views: SAP can rearrange it, and your app doesn't notice.
  • Clean core. Clean core is the promise of updating the system faster and more often than before, allowing companies to use the new technologies instead of waiting years for a hard and difficult system upgrade. To do that, you need to use standard objects. If you have already migrated to S/4, you know what I am talking about needing to adapt the system considering all changes. Using CDS views instead of tables is one step in the clean core approach. 
  • It already speaks Fiori. SAP does the hard work of the joins and associations, so you just use it the way you need, and it's all ready for the day you want an Object Page.

Yes, I know. It's not our language YET, we don't know those CDS names yet, and it's so easy to use a table we know. But remember when VBAK sounded just as weird as I_SalesOrder does now? It stuck because we used it every day. This will stick too, if we choose to start.

Now we have AI to help us speed up our knowledge and search for the right object to select from.  But I always use AI as a co-worker and never as the builder and be sure you add on the prompt to use best practices and use Standard objects whenever possible

So let’s go for it! Creating the CDS on Eclipse…

CDS Code 

@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED //Authorization is not required
@EndUserText.label: 'Demo for ABAP Class' //Just a text
@Metadata.ignorePropagatedAnnotations: true //
define view entity ZC_DEMO
 as select from I_SalesOrder
{
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 10, importance: #HIGH }] //The field below will be the first (10) column on the report
     @UI.selectionField: [{ position: 10 }] //The field below will be on the app as a search field
 key SalesOrder,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 20 }]
     SalesOrderType,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 30 }]
     SalesOrganization,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 40 }]
     @UI.selectionField: [{ position: 20 }]
     CreationDate,
     @UI.lineItem:       [{ position: 50, label: 'Created Today' }]
     @ObjectModel.virtualElement: true //The field below will use an virtual Element
     @ObjectModel.virtualElementCalculatedBy: 'ABAP:ZCL_VIRT_DEMO' //This is the Class you use to calculate the field below
     cast( ' ' as abap.char(1) ) as CreatedToday
}
where CreationDate >= dats_add_days( $session.system_date, -30, 'NULL' ) //Just select the last 30 days

UI annotations: how the backend tells the frontend what to draw

The Fiori app doesn’t know anything about our fields. The annotations in the CDS are instructions that travel with the OData service, and Fiori elements reads them to build the screen.

In plain English: the CDS doesn’t only deliver the data, it also sends instructions to the screen the user interacts with: “Hey, look, here is what you show in the table and here is what you show in the filters.” 

 In our code:

  • @UI.lineItem: this field becomes a column in the report.
  • @UI.selectionField: this field becomes a filter in the filter bar at the top.

The position number sets the order: 10 comes first, then 20, and so on.

Note: I prefer using a Metadata Extension (a separate file that keeps the annotations out of the CDS view), but I really want to keep this very simple here.

Step 2: Create the Virtual Class

Note: I know we could get this logic using a CASE in the CDS, but the idea here is to show how to use the class in a very simple example that everybody understand 😉

This part here is important, so let's translate what this part of the code is saying: 

"Hey CDS, this field will use a virtual element. The value will be calculated by an ABAP class called ZCL_VIRT_DEMO. If nothing is returned, the value is blank. The field will contain a value of 1 char (ABAP CHAR1) and will be exposed as CreatedToday. Nice. See you in the class!" 

So now we need to create the virtual class. 

 

The code

CLASS zcl_virt_demo DEFINITION
 PUBLIC                      "Can be used by other objects
 FINAL                       "Cannot be inherited
 CREATE PUBLIC.
 PUBLIC SECTION.
   "This makes the class a calculator for virtual elements
   INTERFACES if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read.
ENDCLASS.
CLASS zcl_virt_demo IMPLEMENTATION.
 "STEP 1 - Runs FIRST, before the database read.
 "Which real fields do you need to calculate your virtual field?"
 METHOD if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read~get_calculation_info.
   "Only if the app really asked for CreatedToday (names come in UPPERCASE)
   IF line_exists( it_requested_calc_elements[ table_line = 'CREATEDTODAY' ] ).
     "Tell SADL to also read CreationDate from the database
     APPEND 'CREATIONDATE' TO et_requested_orig_elements.
   ENDIF.
 ENDMETHOD.
 "STEP 2 - Runs AFTER the database read, once per package of rows.
 "Here we fill the virtual field.
 METHOD if_sadl_exit_calc_element_read~calculate.
   "Table typed with the CDS view, so we can access fields by name
   DATA lt_orders TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF zc_demo WITH DEFAULT KEY.
   "Copy the generic data into our typed table
   lt_orders = CORRESPONDING #( it_original_data ).
   "Read the date once, outside the loop (no need to ask on every row)
   DATA(lv_today) = cl_abap_context_info=>get_system_date( ).
   LOOP AT lt_orders ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<order>).
     "Created today? Mark with 'X'
     IF <order>-creationdate = lv_today.
       <order>-createdtoday = 'X'.
     ENDIF.
   ENDLOOP.
   "Give the result back to SADL (same rows, same order)
   ct_calculated_data = CORRESPONDING #( lt_orders ).
 ENDMETHOD.
ENDCLASS.

How to debug it

Go to SE24 and search for the class you created. 

Double-click the method you want to debug and create an EXTERNAL breakpoint. 

Important

You can preview the data in Eclipse, right? Yes, but there the class will not be called, and the virtual element comes back blank. Don’t do what I did: I thought my class wasn’t working and spent a long time trying to understand why! Let me save you the trouble: to see the class running, you need to create the service definition, the service binding and the app. 

Step 3: Service Definition and Service Binding

Service Definition - You tell the OData service (the object that selects the data) what you want to be displayed in the result. 

The Code

@EndUserText.label: 'Service Definition for ZC_DEMO'
define service ZUI_DEMO {
 expose ZC_DEMO;
}

Service Binding - You expose the service definition as an OData V4 UI service, so the app can consume your CDS data. 

Activate

When it does not activate

Depending on the architecture of your system, you might not be able to publish your service in Eclipse. If this is your case and you are using V4, you need to go to tcode /n/IWFND/V4_ADMIN. 

Search for your Service Binding, select it and publish it. 

Go back to Eclipse and you will see that the binding is now published.

Step 4: Creating a List Report Page

Just leave the project attributes as they are and finish the project.

You will get a message like the one below:

When it finishes, you will get this message:

  • Open Folder means you will only get this project in BAS.
  • Add Project to Workspace means it will be added to your other projects in BAS. I always use this option. 

Then you can preview the application by right clicking on webapp

The terminal will run and another tab will open with your app! Voilá!

Step 5 - Adding a UI5 element on top of the report

 Until here things went smoothly, but I want to add a Radial Micro Chart on top of the report. So my first instinct was to look for the controller and the view, but there was no MVC… WHAT??????? 

But first, what is MVC?

If you don't know what MVC means and you are an ABAPer, please read this blog post:  Getting cozy with familiar ABAP terms on your new BTP neighborhood 

It was a surprise to me, and then I thought: "Wait... does every template have completely different code and a completely different way of developing?" Gosh! 😅 (Actually, I said a bad word, but let's keep this blog civilized.)

But, as I mentioned in my previous blog Overwhelmed by SAP's new everything? Read this before you give up! I moved from being overwhelmed to being curious, and this time I was curious about how I would add the logic in the backend and not in the frontend.

So I asked Claude and, after a long discussion and a lot of changes, we decided that the best option was to create a Basic app because it was more familiar to me (my first 2 apps were created using Basic Template; be aware that to get to those 2 apps I created like 10 hahahaha).

The main point was that it was very simple to achieve parts of this using the List Report Page, but I couldn't make my UI5 element show up in the app using a custom UI5 extension (a controller file I added to the app), which probably says more about me than about the template. If you know the trick, please tell me. And with the Basic Template, I was trying to reinvent the wheel way too hard.

Then I was like: "There is NO WAY no one wanted to do this before and it is this hard!!"

Trust AI but learn your stuff

I started investigating it. I have taken lots and lots of SAP courses over the course of my career, and many were focused on UX, so I knew about the floorplans. Let's be honest here: it's so easy to think that AI knows more than you do! I think this is going to be the learning curve with this tool: understanding that your expertise matters more than you think.

So I learned that there is something called the Analytical List Page (ALP). The ALP is exactly the combination I was after: KPIs on top, report below. EXACTLY what I need. Claude never suggested it to me until I suggested it to Claude, and then it said that it was obvious that ALP was the best option 😅

What did I learn from this project? 

The nicest thing about being new at something is that once you overcome the first aversion to the new, you learn a lot very fast and mostly by making mistakes. With this project I tried a custom UI5 extension, two new floorplans, an ABAP class in a CDS, an analytical data definition and more.

Now I know when to use an Analytical List Page and when to use a List Report Page. List Report when the goal is to list and filter. ALP when you want KPIs and charts on top, working together with the list below. 

I tried to summarize it all here so you could learn from my experience. Let me know if it worked! 😉

——————

While this post might be basic to some, I added here everything that was getting me overwhelmed for years and all my questions related to those things. My goal with these posts is to demystify the new SAP development world together with you.

I'll continue sharing simple posts based on real discoveries, real questions and real experiences, sharing my journey, my learnings and my bumps along the way so you don't need to go through some of them yourself.

If you're in the same boat, stay tuned. There will be many more posts about this journey.

If you're further along than this, pretty please help us in the comments.

To be continued

I’m on holiday now, in Brazil to be more exact , so there’s no ALP update yet (yes, I’m still writing here, apparently I can’t help it 😅). But I will write about the Analytical List Page as soon as I’m back and get it sorted. And I promise to tell you honestly what worked and what didn’t. 

Thanks for reading!

entry.title: CDS View Performance Best Practice – UNION in a LEFT OUTER JOIN
entry.content:
UNION in a LEFT OUTER JOIN -  CDS (SQL) performance anti-pattern

This blog post focuses on the CDS view performance anti-pattern called "UNION in LEFT OUTER JOIN" and it's part of the CDS View Performance Best Practices series. You can find an introduction to CDS View performance recommendations, aspects you need to consider in terms of performance, and a list of all available CDS anti-patterns in the following blog post: 
CDS View Performance Best Practices 

 

Why this pattern deserves attention

A UNION in the right-hand input of a LEFT OUTER JOIN is logically valid. The risk is performance: on large data volumes and complex data models, both UNION branches may be processed before a selective filter from the left side of the join can reduce them. In simple and highly selective cases, the optimizer may apply semi-join reduction. In more complex plans, that optimization is not guaranteed because plan selection is cost based.

 

The business example

A retail company tracks customer orders for multiple sales regions. Each order is fulfilled through one of two independent delivery systems: a central warehouse or a regional warehouse. Fulfillment is exclusive in this model: an order is only assigned to one delivery system. Some orders are still open and therefore have no delivery record. The data below is intentionally minimal so that result of every row can be easily followed through each query variant by hand.

Data model

The following three tables are created and populated by the complete runnable SQL at the end of this post. All rows are shown so every query result can be verified by hand.

Table: ORDERS

ORDER_ID

REGION_ID

ORD100

1

ORD200

1

ORD300

2

ORD400

2

ORD500

2

 ORD400 is still open and has no delivery in either system and therefore is not part of the following tables.

Table: CENTRAL_DELIVERIES

ORDER_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD100

2026-09-10

ORD300

2026-09-15

ORD900

2026-08-20

 ORD900 is an older, delivered order that is not part of the current ORDERS selection.

Table: REGIONAL_DELIVERIES

ORDER_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD200

2026-09-12

ORD500

2026-09-18

ORD950

2026-08-25

 ORD950 is another older, delivered order that is not part of the current ORDERS selection.

 

The original, correct query

The query goal is to list every order together with its delivery date from Region 2 (region_id = 2), regardless of which delivery system handled it. Open orders must still appear with a NULL delivery date — the LEFT OUTER JOIN is the mechanism that guarantees this.

with deliveries as (
    select order_id, delivery_date
      from central_deliveries
    union all
    select order_id, delivery_date
      from regional_deliveries
)
select o.order_id,
       o.region_id,
       d.delivery_date
  from orders o
  left outer join deliveries d
    on o.order_id = d.order_id
 where o.region_id = 2;

Please note that the query uses a common table expression (CTE). The with_clause creates a temporary result set based on its subquery. The native SQL approach uses the WITH clause for simplicity, avoiding multiple view definitions and lengthy code snippets while showing the essence of the anti-pattern in a single executable statement.

Technically, this has the same effect as when a CDS view uses an association (technically a LEFT OUTER JOIN) to another CDS view that contains a UNION.

 The main query selects from the table ORDERS and uses the temporary view (CTE) DELIVERIES in a LEFT OUTER JOIN. The CTE  DELIVERIES contains a UNION ALL of the two delivery tables CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES.

Correct and expected result of the query:

ORDER_ID

REGION_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD300

2

2026-09-15

ORD400

2

NULL

ORD500

2

2026-09-18

 

Let’s look at the execution plan for the query.

The plan places the UNION ALL below the LEFT OUTER JOIN, this means the UNION ALL is executed before the LEFT OUTER JOIN. The filtered ORDERS table is the left input, while CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES are combined as the right input.

The UNION ALL combines the rows from both delivery tables so that an order can match a delivery stored in either table. The LEFT OUTER JOIN then keeps every selected Region 2 order, including ORD400, for which neither table contains a delivery record.

The plan does not show the selected order IDs being used to reduce the scans of CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and REGIONAL_DELIVERIES. Rows that cannot match a selected order are therefore processed.

Can the filtered ORDERS input and the LEFT OUTER JOIN be pushed into the individual UNION ALL branches to reduce the data earlier?

 

The tempting but incorrect rewrite

At first glance, it may seem attractive to push the filtered ORDERS input and the LEFT OUTER JOIN into each UNION ALL branch:

with deliveries_wrong_opt as (
    select o.order_id, o.region_id,
           cd.delivery_date
      from orders o
      left outer join central_deliveries cd
        on o.order_id = cd.order_id
     where o.region_id = 2
    union all
    select o.order_id, o.region_id,
           rd.delivery_date
      from orders o
      left outer join regional_deliveries rd
        on o.order_id = rd.order_id
     where o.region_id = 2
)
select * from deliveries_wrong_opt;

Why it fails: Each LEFT OUTER JOIN independently preserves every selected order. ORD300 has a matching row in CENTRAL_DELIVERIES, but not in REGIONAL_DELIVERIES therefore the regional branch produces a NULL-extended row for it. ORD500 has the symmetric problem. ORD400 has no match in either delivery table, so both branches produce a NULL-extended row for it.

The UNION ALL then combines the independently produced branch results. Consequently, the rewritten query returns six rows instead of the expected three. The additional rows are not caused by UNION ALL itself; they arise because each LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched orders independently.

ORDER_ID

REGION_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD300

2

2026-09-15

ORD300

2

NULL

ORD400

2

NULL

ORD400

2

NULL

ORD500

2

NULL

ORD500

2

2026-09-18

The execution plan shows both the performance appeal and the structural problem of this rewrite:

The UNION ALL is now above two separate LEFT OUTER JOIN operators. Each branch reads the filtered Region 2 rows from ORDERS and joins them independently with one delivery table: the first branch with CENTRAL_DELIVERIES and the second with REGIONAL_DELIVERIES. Because only the selected orders participate in each join, fewer rows may be passed from the join branches into the UNION ALL.

The earlier reduction therefore looks attractive from a performance perspective, but it changes the result. Because both joins are LEFT OUTER JOINs, each branch preserves all three Region 2 orders before the branch results are combined. A match in one branch does not prevent the other branch from producing a NULL-extended row for the same order. For this data set, the UNION ALL consequently receives three rows from each branch and returns the six rows shown above.

If the LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot be pushed down into the UNION ALL branches, can the delivery tables still be reduced earlier without changing the result?

 

A semantics-preserving manual reduction

The LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot safely be pushed down into the UNION ALL branches. Therefore, we describe an approach where the selected order IDs can be used to reduce each delivery table before the tables are combined.

The query first creates selected_order_keys, containing the order IDs for Region 2. Each delivery table is then joined with these IDs, so only deliveries for the selected orders enter the UNION ALL. The LEFT OUTER JOIN remains in the main query and therefore still returns open orders, such as ORD400, exactly once.

with selected_order_keys as (
    select distinct order_id
      from orders
     where region_id = 2
),
reduced_deliveries as (
    select d.order_id, d.delivery_date
      from central_deliveries d
      inner join selected_order_keys k
        on k.order_id = d.order_id
    union all
    select d.order_id, d.delivery_date
      from regional_deliveries d
      inner join selected_order_keys k
        on k.order_id = d.order_id
)
select o.order_id,
       o.region_id,
       d.delivery_date
  from orders o
  left outer join reduced_deliveries d
    on d.order_id = o.order_id
 where o.region_id = 2;

The DISTINCT ensures that each order ID occurs only once in selected_order_keys. Otherwise, duplicate IDs could multiply matching rows in the delivery tables.

This query produces the correct and expected result:

ORDER_ID

REGION_ID

DELIVERY_DATE

ORD300

2

2026-09-15

ORD400

2

NULL

ORD500

2

2026-09-18

The result remains the same as for the original query, but unrelated delivery rows are removed before the UNION ALL. The execution plan below shows how SAP HANA implements this reduction.

The filtered Region 2 order IDs are produced once by the DISTINCT operator and reused as a shared subplan. Each delivery table is then reduced through a HASH JOIN (SEMI): only delivery rows whose ORDER_ID occurs in selected_order_keys are passed to the UNION ALL. The resulting delivery rows form the right-hand input of the final HASH JOIN (LEFT OUTER).

The semi-joins reduce the delivery branches without producing NULL-extended order rows. Preserving unmatched orders remains the responsibility of the single LEFT OUTER JOIN above the UNION ALL. The plan therefore combines early reduction with the same result semantics as the original query.

The manual rewrite makes the reduction explicit by deriving the relevant order IDs and using them to restrict both delivery branches.

But is this manual rewrite always necessary, or can SAP HANA derive the same semi-join reduction automatically?

 

How SAP HANA can apply semi-join reduction automatically

The fact that the LEFT OUTER JOIN cannot be pushed down does not automatically imply poor performance. SAP HANA can introduce semi-join reduction as an optimizer transformation without changing the SQL statement. Whether it does so is cost based and depends on estimated cardinalities, internal cost evaluation rules, selectivity, table sizes, statistics, and the complexity of the execution plan resulting from the surrounding data model.

In the small teaching example used so far, the delivery tables contain only a few rows. Reducing them first offers little or no cost advantage, so SAP HANA may reasonably retain the original plan.

With larger data volumes, reducing rows before the UNION ALL can provide enough benefit for the optimizer to choose semi-join reduction automatically. The following example demonstrates this with large SAP tables.

Example with large SAP tables

Table

Description

Approximate number of rows

TADIR

Directory of ABAP Repository objects. It provides the object type, object name, and package assignment.

7 million

DD03L

Contains field information for ABAP Dictionary tables and structures.

15 million

DD03ND

Contains field information for structured Dictionary objects, including objects related to CDS data definitions.

2.5 million

Purpose of the query

The query selects the names and types of table definitions (TABL) and CDS data definitions (DDLS) assigned to package FINS_CODING_BLOCK in TADIR. It combines field information from DD03L and DD03ND with UNION ALL and left-joins the result to the selected repository objects.

The LEFT OUTER JOIN ensures that repository objects without matching field information are still returned. Objects with multiple fields produce one result row per field.

with fields as (
    select d.tabname as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03l d

    union all

    select d.strucobjn as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03nd d
)
select t.object,
       t.obj_name,
       f.fieldname
  from tadir t
  left outer join fields f
    on f.objectname = t.obj_name
 where t.devclass = 'FINS_CODING_BLOCK'
   and t.object in ('TABL', 'DDLS');

Execution with automatic semi-join reduction

For runtime measurements we will use Plan Visualizer (PlanViz) instead of the explain plan. If we create the execution plan for the query using PlanViz we can find the following time measurements on the Overview tab in the execution summary section:

Execution Time (Elapsed): 4.524 ms
Execution Time (CPU): 3.771 ms

The Plan Graph view of the PlanViz looks like this:

The filtered TADIR input is evaluated once and reused as a shared subplan. The filter returns 48 rows, compared with an estimate (by the optimizer) of 12 rows (number in parentheses). The operator times shown in this Plan Graph are CPU times, not elapsed times.

SAP HANA uses this selective result to apply a TABLE SCAN SEMI JOIN to both branches below the UNION ALL. The semi-join on DD03L passes 222 rows to the UNION ALL, while the semi-join on DD03ND passes 196 rows. Only rows with an object name that occurs in the filtered TADIR result are passed to the UNION ALL.

The UNION ALL combines the two branch results into 418 rows. These rows form the right-hand input of the final HASH JOIN (LEFT OUTER), while the filtered TADIR result remains the left-hand input. The outer join therefore continues to preserve selected repository objects without matching field information.

The plan demonstrates automatic semi-join reduction: SAP HANA uses the selective left-side input to reduce both large field tables before their rows are combined, without moving the LEFT OUTER JOIN into the UNION ALL branches. The measured CPU time for this run is approximately 3.8 ms.

The plan shows that SAP HANA reduces both field tables before the UNION ALL. But how much work does this transformation avoid? To make the difference visible, we can execute the same statement once more with semi-join reduction disabled and compare the two PlanViz results.

Execution with automatic semi-join reduction disabled

To isolate the effect of semi-join reduction, the same statement was executed again with the hint NO_HEX_TABLE_SCAN_SEMI_JOIN that prevents the table-scan semi-join reduction in the individual UNION ALL branches. The hint is used only for demonstration; disabling the optimization is not recommended.

with fields as (
    select d.tabname as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03l d

    union all

    select d.strucobjn as objectname,
           d.fieldname
      from dd03nd d
)
select t.object,
       t.obj_name,
       f.fieldname
  from tadir t
  left outer join fields f
    on f.objectname = t.obj_name
 where t.devclass = 'FINS_CODING_BLOCK'
   and t.object in ('TABL', 'DDLS') 
WITH HINT( NO_HEX_TABLE_SCAN_SEMI_JOIN );

The following time measurements are from the overview in the execution summary:

Execution Time (Elapsed): 472.078 ms
Execution Time (CPU): 7,291.854 ms

Compared to the previous optimized execution we can see significantly higher times.


Execution Time (Elapsed): 4.524 ms
Execution Time (CPU): 3.771 ms

The Plan Graph view looks like this:

With branch-level semi-join reduction disabled, the filtered TADIR input is still evaluated once and reused as a shared subplan. The filter returns 48 rows.

The main difference is visible below the UNION ALL. Semi-join reduction has not disappeared completely, but it now occurs above the UNION ALL. Consequently, both large field tables are scanned and combined before the result is reduced to the selected object names. The DD03L scan returns 15,747,433 rows, while the DD03ND scan returns 2,495,229 rows.

These large branch results enter the UNION ALL before a HASH JOIN (SEMI) reduces the combined field data to the object names from the filtered TADIR input. The semi-join eventually reduces the data to 418 rows, but the reduction happens only after rows from both large tables have already been read and combined.

The resulting 418 rows form the right-hand input of the final HASH JOIN (LEFT OUTER). As in the optimized plan, the filtered TADIR result remains the left-hand input, so repository objects without matching field information are still preserved. The final result therefore remains unchanged. The measured CPU time for this run is approximately 7.3 s.

Comparison of the two executions

Measurement

Semi-join reduction enabled

Branch-level reduction disabled

Rows from DD03L entering UNION ALL

222

15,747,433

Rows from DD03ND entering UNION ALL

196

2,495,229

Total rows entering UNION ALL

418

18,242,662

Final result rows

418

418

Approximate elapsed time

4.5 ms

472 ms

Approximate CPU time

3.8 ms

7.3 s

Both executions return the same 418 rows, but the optimized plan reduces each field table before the UNION ALL. This avoids passing more than 18 million rows through the union and reduces CPU time from approximately 7.3 seconds to 3.8 milliseconds. But what can a developer do if SAP HANA does not apply semi-join reduction and the UNION branches become a performance bottleneck?

 

When semi-join reduction is not applied

Semi-join reduction is a cost-based optimizer decision. It may not be selected when the left-side filter is insufficiently selective, cardinality estimates are inaccurate, or join columns contain casts or calculations. The structure of the data model also matters: additional joins, aggregations, calculated fields, and nested (reusable) views can increase the complexity of the resulting execution plan and make the relationship between the selective input and the UNION branches harder for the optimizer to identify.

This is one reason why controlling CDS model complexity is important. For broader guidance, see CDS View Performance Best Practices.

Use PlanViz with representative data volumes to check where rows are reduced, how many rows enter the UNION ALL, and whether estimated row counts differ significantly from the actual values.

What can a developer do?

  • If the branches use the same source rows at the same granularity and differ only in calculated values, consider replacing the union with a single source and CASE expressions. Verify that this preserves row multiplicity and NULL handling (see anti-pattern NOT NULL preserving LEFT OUTER JOIN).
  • Consider separate, more focused views when a broadly reusable union model prevents early filtering.
  • For expensive and stable combinations, consider whether a persisted or precomputed result is appropriate.
  • Verify every redesign with PlanViz and realistic production-scale data.

The objective is not to force a particular execution plan, but to shape the data model so that SAP HANA can reduce large data sets as early as possible.

 

Conclusion

A UNION ALL on the right side of a LEFT OUTER JOIN is logically valid, but it can become expensive when large union branches are processed before the selective left-side input reduces them. Simply moving the LEFT OUTER JOIN into the individual branches is not a safe optimization and leads to a semantically different result, because each branch would preserve unmatched rows.

SAP HANA can avoid this work through semi-join reduction, restricting the union branches while keeping the LEFT OUTER JOIN above the UNION. If this optimization is not applied and the union becomes a performance bottleneck, review the CDS model for opportunities to reduce data earlier without changing row multiplicity or NULL handling. Use PlanViz with representative data volumes to identify the problem and verify any redesign.

entry.title: Update SAP Table Maintenance Generator (TMG) After Table Structure Changes Without Deleting It
entry.content:
Introduction

In SAP ABAP development, the Table Maintenance Generator (TMG) provides a standard way to maintain table entries through transaction SM30. It allows users to create, modify, and delete records without developing a separate maintenance program.

A common challenge occurs when a new field is added to a custom table that already has a TMG. The updated field may not appear in the existing maintenance screen.

One approach is to delete and recreate the TMG. However, if the existing maintenance dialog contains custom event logic or screen modifications, recreating it can introduce additional rework.

In this blog, we will explore how to update an existing TMG using the generation settings in SAP, without unnecessarily deleting the existing maintenance object.

Prerequisites

Before starting, ensure that:

  • You have an existing custom table with an active TMG.

  • The table is maintained through transaction SM30.

  • You have the required development authorizations.

  • Any existing TMG events or screen modifications have been documented.

Step 1: Check the Existing Table Maintenance Screen

Open transaction SM30 and enter the custom table or maintenance view name.

Choose Maintain to display the current maintenance screen. Note the existing fields and any custom functionality.

Step 2: Add the New Field to the Table

Open transaction SE11 and enter the custom table name.

Choose Change, add the required field to the table definition, maintain its data element and other relevant properties, and activate the table.

If the change requires a database adjustment, assess the impact and perform the necessary adjustment using the appropriate SAP tools and procedures.

Step 3: Open the Existing Table Maintenance Generator

While working with the table in SE11, navigate to:

Utilities → Table Maintenance Generator

Open the existing maintenance generator configuration and choose Change.

The objective is to adjust the existing generated maintenance dialog rather than delete the maintenance object and recreate it from scratch.

Step 4: Select the Appropriate Structure Change Option

In the generation settings, select the option corresponding to the structural change you have made.

For adding a field, select:

New field/sec. table in structure

If a field has been removed, choose the corresponding option for a field or secondary table removed from the structure.

Proceed to the next screen.

Step 5: Review the Field and Screen Settings

Continue through the generation wizard and verify the relevant settings.

Depending on your existing maintenance dialog, confirm:

  • Whether the new field is a key field or a non-key field.

  • Whether the maintenance dialog uses a one-step or two-step layout.

  • Whether the existing screen arrangement remains appropriate.

  • Whether any custom screen changes need to be preserved or reviewed.

Select the options that match your table design and proceed.

Step 6: Complete the Generation Adjustment

Continue through the remaining confirmation screens. Allow SAP to process the changes, then save the updated maintenance configuration.

Check the system messages and resolve any errors before moving to validation.

The exact screens and available options may vary depending on the SAP release and maintenance object configuration.

Step 7: Validate the Changes in SM30

Return to transaction SM30 and open the same table or maintenance view in change mode.

Verify that:

  1. The newly added field is available on the maintenance screen.

  2. Existing fields are displayed correctly.

  3. New and existing records can be maintained as expected.

  4. Relevant custom TMG events continue to behave correctly.

  5. Saving the entries updates the data as intended.

Important Considerations

  • Preserve custom logic: Review existing TMG events and screen modifications before changing generation settings.

  • Validate key changes carefully: Adding or removing key fields can affect maintenance behavior and existing records.

  • Test before transporting: Perform the required functional and regression testing in the development and quality systems.

  • Do not assume every modification is preserved automatically: Custom screen layouts, generated objects, and event implementations should be checked after the adjustment.

Conclusion

When a table structure changes, deleting and recreating the entire Table Maintenance Generator should not be the first option.

By reviewing the existing TMG configuration and selecting the appropriate structure-change settings, you can update the maintenance dialog while reducing unnecessary rework.

Always validate the resulting SM30 screen and existing custom functionality before transporting the changes to another system.

entry.title: CDS Table Entities - Definition of Fields: built-in types and type mappings
entry.content:
The next two parts of the series will dive deeper into field definitions in CDS table entities; this article starting out with ABAP built-in types, and the next focusing on data elements and CDS types. In case you missed the previous post, "Getting Started with CDS Table Entities", you can read it here.

How to define fields in CDS table entities

Table entities are composed of a list of field definitions, all of which follow the structure:

field_definition ::=
    [field_annotation]
    [key] field_name : type_reference [null];

An example field list could look like this:

@ClientHandling.type: #CLIENT_DEPENDENT
@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass: #APPLICATION_DATA
@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'Mountains of the world'
define table entity ZAK_MOUNTAINS
{
  key mountain_id    : abap.raw(16);
      mountain_name  : abap.char(80);
      mountain_range : abap.char(30);
      description    : abap.string null; 
      @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure: 'height_unit'
      height      : abap.quan(7,2);
      height_unit : abap.unit;      
      first_ascent   : abap.datn; // date of first ascent
      first_ascent_at : abap.utclong; // timestamp of first ascent
      num_routes   : abap.int4;   // known routes to the summit  
      @Semantics.spatialData.srid.value: '0'
      location : abap.geom_ewkb null; 
}

As you can see above, the syntax is still very similar to how fields are defined in classic dictionary tables. Primary key fields are defined with the keyword key, just like one would expect it in classic tables as well.

Fields that contain the keyword null are nullable, meaning these columns may contain SQL null values. Unlike classic tables, CDS table entities officially support nullability. The reason for this is that some datatypes do not have a suitable default value on the database, so they require the null keyword when used in the field definition (a more detailed post on this topic will follow later).

While classic tables contain an explicit client field with type mandt in their field list, CDS table entities handle client dependency implicitly, similarly to CDS view entities. This means that it is no longer necessary to define an explicit client field in the field list. Instead, client dependency is handled via header annotation @ClientHandling.type (more on this will follow in a dedicated article as well). This change in behavior was motivated by two factors: First, aligning the client handling behavior with CDS view entities rather than classic tables leads to more consistency in terms of behavior across different CDS objects. And secondly, since the client field does not contain any true business payload but rather a system-managed key for tenant isolation, it is not necessary to declare it explicitly in the data model.

Numeric types

Let’s start with the easiest kind of datatype: the numeric types. The following numeric built-in types are supported in CDS table entities:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.int1

INT1

b (1-byte int)

TINYINT

abap.int2

INT2

s (2-byte int)

SMALLINT

abap.int4

INT4

i (4-byte int)

INTEGER

abap.int8

INT8

int8

BIGINT

abap.dec

DEC

p (packed)

DECIMAL

abap.decfloat16

DECFLOAT16

decfloat16

SMALLDECIMAL

abap.decfloat34

DECFLOAT34

decfloat34

DECIMAL

abap.fltp

FLTP

f (float)

DOUBLE

It should be noted that in classic tables, abap.int1 is mapped to SMALLINT, whereas CDS table entities map this type tp TINYINT. Not only does this save space (which is precious!), it also results in congruent domains in ABAP and the database. This datatype is the only case so far where the type mapping differs between classic tables and CDS table entities.

While abap.dec and abap.decfloat34 are both mapped to DECIMAL on HANA, these two are fundamentally different types with different behavior. The type abap.dec requires two arguments, declaring an explicit length and decimal places via precision (p) and scale (s). The resulting HANA type is therefore a fixed-point DECIMAL(p,s) with hard maximum of p total digits and exactly s fractional digits.
On the other hand, abap.decfloat34 does not have any arguments. It maps to a decimal floating-point number where the precision and scale of the stored value are determined by the value itself. This difference has some practical implications, for example when performing a CAST operation between dec and decfloat34 in CDS.
Similarly, the smaller datatype abap.decfloat16, which is mapped to SMALLDECIMAL, also represents a floating-point decimal. However, unlike abap.decfloat34 which has a capacity of 16 bytes with up to 34 decimal digits, abap.decfloat16 only has a capacity for 8 bytes with up to 16 decimal digits in its coefficient.
Lastly, columns typed as abap.fltp store binary floating-point numbers, meaning only integer powers of 2 can be represented exactly. This can lead to ambiguities and  rounding errors (e.g., after divisions by powers of 10), which is also the reason abap.fltp cannot be used as datatype for key fields in CDS.

Since developing new objects always comes with getting rid of some old pain points from the past, we chose to deprecate some types as well:

While types DF16_DEC and DF34_DEC (decimal floating point stored in binary coded decimal format) can be changed to type DEC without adjustments on the database, DF16_RAW and DF34_RAW (stored in binary format) require a table conversion to be changed to DEC or DECFLOAT16 or DECFLOAT34, respectively. DF16_SCL and DF34_SCL (stored in binary format with specific scaling) as well as PREC are officially obsolete. Since HANA has native built-in decfloat support, the old decfloat types listed above are no longer needed and therefore deprecated.

Character-like types

The following character-like types are supported as well:

Supported types:

abap.char

NVARCHAR

LANG

NVARCHAR

In CDS table entites, abap.string will no longer have a length component besides abap.string(0) (a length of zero means „unlimited length“). This means we always consider strings to have no length limits. An important distinction however is that "no length limit" does not mean "infinite storage". It simply means that the type itself does not impose a limit to how long a string value can be. The underlying NCLOB column in the database still has a physical ceiling which belongs to the infrastructure layer.
Due to the lack of suitable default values for NCLOBS on the database, abap.string is also denoted as a nullable type, i.e., it is one of the datatypes which require the null keyword (along with abap.rawstring, see below). Not adding this keyword will result in syntax errors.
Unlike abap.string, abap.sstring can also be used in where clauses, join conditions and indices.

Can‘t we just use NUMC for every number? – Our recommendations

The datatype abap.numc is one of the most frequently used types, e.g. to denote different kinds of IDs such as buyer IDs or item numbers. It is a character-like type that accepts only digits, and maps to NVARCHAR on the database just like any other CHAR-like type. Since abap.numc is digit-only and auto-pads with leading zeros, it appears more controlled at handling numbers than a plain CHARat first glance. However, it lacks all of the actual semantics of numeric types (such as arithmetic, ordering, or range checks). Overusing abap.numc can therefore lead to potential problems:

  • Since NUMC is a character-like type on the database, SQL aggregations such as AVG, SUM or MAX cannot be used on NUMC-fields. Moreover, there isn’t any digit-only enforcement on the database either: In the old dynpro world, screen field validation would at least catch non-digit input at the UI layer, however, In a RAP/Fiori Elements world, that enforcement is gone unless you explicitly add a validation in the behavior definition.
  • Comparisons with other CHAR-fields may lead to unexpected results due to implicit conversion rules if the CHAR-field is not purely numeric (e. g., in where-clauses).
  • NUMC-fields of different lengths are not cast-compatible (e. g. abap.numc(5) and abap.numc(6)), resulting in errors when attempting to join similar looking „numbers“ across different entities.
  • NUMC is only compatible with CHAR and other NUMC fields of equal or greater length in comparisons and ON-conditions. For example, defining a NUMC key in a child entity and attempting to join it to a parent which contains a NUMC-field of a different length will result in an activation error. It can only be fixed by realigning lengths, which may even require a table migration if the table already contains data.
  • Using NUMC in Native SQL and AMDP is explicitly discouraged in the docs, as conversions in the Native SQL interface should be avoided whenever possible.
  • NUMC fields in OData services typically need explicit handling to avoid the leading zeros being stripped, or the field being mistyped on the consumer side.

There is a legitimate use case for abap.numc though, which is whenever there are fixed-length numeric identifiers where leading zeros are part of the business meaning (e.g., as item or order numbers). For other use cases, we recommend the following:

  • For technical primary key fields, you can use the data element UUID for example (which has base type RAW(16)) rather than NUMC. UUID keys enable managed early numbering, meaning the RAP framework generates them automatically in the BDEF and no custom numbering logic is needed. In unmanaged BOs or classic ABAP, UUIDs can be generated via CL_SYSTEM_UUID directly, while in ABAP Cloud/BTP you can use the XCO library as well.
  • For counters or internal sequences, actual numeric types such as abap.int4 should be used instead.
  • For fiscal years or posting periods, we recommend using a DATN column instead. If for some reason this is not possible, the more suitable alternative would be using dedicated data elements or CDS types which have NUMC as their base type, but feature proper conversion exits as well. For data elements they can be directly included in the domain, while in CDS types they are added via annotation AbapCatalog.typeSpec.conversionExit.
  • For digit sequences such as postal codes, abap.char is the more future-proof choice in case letters need to be added later.
  • Any field which is exposed in OData should have also a CHAR-type instead of NUMC to avoid the need for extra handling of the leading zeros.

Lastly, some character-like types are also no longer supported in CDS table entities:

NVARCHAR

The type abap.clnt is known for being used solely for client fields. However, since we no longer denote client fields explicitly, we chose to no longer support this type either to avoid confusion.

The issue with abap.lchr is that this type requires the field length to be declared as an additional INT-field right before the LCHR, which is already impractical. Additionally, there can be only one such LCHR field in a table, and both the INT- and LCHR fields have to be the last columns at the end of the table. Since this type has no advantages on the database, we recommend using abap.string or abap.sstring instead, which map to proper LOB column types in HANA and get the job done just as well.

Currency and quantity types

One of the most frequent use cases is denoting currency and quantity fields. All the currency and quantity types you are already familiar with are supported in CDS table entities and mapped as follows:

The element annotations @Semantics.amount and @Semantics.quantity  are of course still mandatory when using abap.curr and abap.quan respectively, since activation will fail without them.


Date and time

For date and time formats, we decided to only support the more modern types abap.datn, abap.timn and abap.utclong/abap.utcl, while deprecating the „old“ types abap.dats, abap.tims and abap.accp. An overview can be seen below:

Supported types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

ABAP Type

HANA DB Type

abap.datn

DATN

d

DATE

abap.timn

abap.utclong

Deprecated types:

ABAP CDS Built-in

DDIC Type

DATS

d
